sections.body:
The channelopathies — LQTS, SQTS, Brugada, and CPVT — cause SCD in structurally normal hearts. Their ECG patterns, triggers, and treatments are completely different from each other. One drug cures CPVT; another kills a Brugada patient. This chapter builds the complete pattern recognition map.

## Long QT syndrome (LQTS)

### The ECG finding

Corrected QT (QTc) >450 ms in men, >460 ms in women. QTc = QT / √RR (Bazett formula). A prolonged QT indicates prolonged phase 3 repolarisation — the ventricle takes longer to repolarise. During this prolonged repolarisation, early afterdepolarisations (EADs) can reach threshold → trigger Torsades de Pointes (TdP).

### Congenital LQTS subtypes — the most testable

| Subtype | Gene / Current affected | Trigger | T-wave morphology | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LQT1 (most common, ~45%) | KCNQ1 — ↓ IKs (slow K⁺ delayed rectifier) | Exercise / swimming (adrenergic) | Broad-based, smooth T waves | Beta-blockers (highly effective — exercise-triggered events suppressed) |
| LQT2 (~40%) | KCNH2 (hERG) — ↓ IKr (rapid K⁺ delayed rectifier) | Auditory triggers (sudden sounds, alarm clocks), emotional stress | Notched, bifid T waves (two humps) | Beta-blockers; avoid K⁺-depleting drugs; DOAC for AF if develops; ICD for high-risk; supplemental K⁺ (raises K⁺ → more IKr available at any level) |
| LQT3 (~10%) | SCN5A — ↑ late INa (slow Na⁺ inactivation) | Rest / sleep (bradycardia-dependent — events at slow HR when QT is longest) | Late-peaking, asymmetric T wave with long isoelectric segment | Mexiletine (class Ib — reduces late INa), ranolazine; beta-blockers less effective; pacing to prevent bradycardia-triggered events; ICD for high-risk |

Key concept: LQT1 events are triggered by exercise → beta-blockers are highly effective. LQT3 events occur at rest/sleep → beta-blockers are less effective and mexiletine targets the mechanism
The trigger specificity of different LQTS subtypes is the most clinically important distinction. LQT1 and LQT2: adrenergic activation increases heart rate → shortens the QT cycle but paradoxically increases the dispersion of repolarisation → EADs → TdP. Beta-blockers reduce the adrenergic trigger → highly effective in LQT1 (85–90% reduction in events). LQT3: slow heart rate at rest/sleep → longer QT intervals → EADs → TdP. Here beta-blockers actually worsen the bradycardia and may increase risk. Mexiletine blocks the "leak" of late INa current that is the LQT3 mechanism → reduces QTc by 40–50 ms in LQT3 → highly specific and effective treatment.

## Brugada syndrome

### ECG pattern

Coved-type ST elevation ≥2 mm in ≥1 right precordial lead (V1–V2), with negative T wave. Must be spontaneous or provoked by class Ia/Ic sodium channel blocker (ajmaline, flecainide, procainamide — these "unmask" a latent Brugada pattern). Type 1 (coved-type) is the only diagnostic ECG. Type 2 (saddle-back) is non-diagnostic without provocation.

### Mechanism

Loss-of-function mutations in SCN5A (sodium channel — ~25–30% of Brugada syndrome). Reduced INa → phase 1 repolarisation in the epicardium is more pronounced (the Ito current dominates → large notch in the epicardial AP) → accentuated epicardial dome in some areas but not others → epicardial-endocardial voltage gradient → ST elevation + risk of phase 2 re-entry → VT/VF. Predominantly affects the RVOT epicardium (explains V1–V2 ST changes).

### Triggers

- Fever (the most common trigger — SCN5A channels become more dysfunctional at high temperatures) → treat fever aggressively in Brugada patients
- Sodium channel blockers (flecainide, ajmaline, cocaine) — unmask or worsen the Brugada pattern
- Sleep / vagal activation / bradycardia
- Large meals (vagal activation post-prandially)
- Hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hypercalcaemia

### Management

- ICD: indicated for symptomatic Brugada (aborted SCA, syncope with documented VT/VF). For asymptomatic Brugada with spontaneous type 1 ECG — risk stratification based on EP study inducibility and other risk features.
- Quinidine (class Ia — blocks Ito outward K⁺ current) → restores the epicardial dome → reduces the transmural voltage gradient → prevents VF in Brugada. Used as adjunct to ICD or when ICD is declined/not available.
- Catheter ablation of the RVOT epicardium (elimination of the trigger area) — emerging evidence, used in centres with experience.
- Avoid: sodium channel blockers (class Ic, Ia), tricyclic antidepressants, large alcohol intake, cannabis (all can provoke Brugada pattern and VF).

## Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT)

Exercise or stress-induced polymorphic VT or bidirectional VT in a structurally normal heart with no QT prolongation. Mechanism: RyR2 (ryanodine receptor 2) mutation → spontaneous Ca²⁺ release from SR during adrenergic stimulation → DADs → triggered VT. Characteristic arrhythmia: bidirectional VT — QRS alternates direction beat-to-beat (RBBB morphology in one beat, LBBB in the next, or alternating axis), only during exercise or catecholamine infusion. Resting ECG is normal.

Treatment:

- Beta-blockers (nadolol preferred — high-dose): suppress adrenergic-triggered Ca²⁺ release. First-line and highly effective.
- Flecainide (class Ic): secondary mechanism — blocks RyR2 directly (in addition to Na⁺ channel block) → reduces spontaneous Ca²⁺ release. Add-on for high-risk patients or when beta-blockers are insufficient. Effective despite being generally avoided in structural heart disease (CPVT has no structural disease).
- ICD for aborted SCA or persistent VT despite medical therapy. ICD shocks → adrenergic surge → more VT → ICD storm → may need beta-blockers + flecainide + sedation to break the cycle.
- Avoid competitive exercise — exercise can trigger lethal arrhythmias.

## Short QT syndrome (SQTS)

QTc ≤320 ms with short QT on ECG. Tall, narrow, symmetric T waves. Gain-of-function mutations in K⁺ channels (KCNH2, KCNQ1) or loss-of-function in Ca²⁺ channels → accelerated repolarisation → short vulnerable window but predisposed to VF. Rare. ICD for symptomatic patients. Quinidine as adjunct (prolongs QT by blocking IKr).

Exam tip: The four channelopathy syndromes — their distinguishing drug treatments: LQT1: beta-blocker (exercise-triggered → suppress adrenergic trigger)
LQT2: beta-blocker + avoid QT-prolonging drugs + K⁺ supplementation
LQT3: mexiletine (blocks late INa — the mutation) ± beta-blocker + pacing
Brugada: quinidine (blocks Ito — restores dome) + ICD; AVOID Na⁺ channel blockers
CPVT: beta-blocker (nadolol) + flecainide (blocks RyR2); AVOID sympathomimetics
Drug crossovers that kill: Flecainide in Brugada = blocks Na⁺ channels → worsens Brugada → VF. Flecainide in CPVT = safe and beneficial. This is not a contradiction — it reflects completely different mechanisms.

Checkpoint: A 20-year-old swimming champion collapses in the pool during a race. She is resuscitated. Her resting ECG shows QTc 520 ms with broad-based T waves in the precordial leads. Her father had unexplained syncope during exercise. What gene is likely mutated, what is her specific treatment priority, and which sport is now absolutely contraindicated?
LQT1. The clue combination is classical: QTc markedly prolonged (520 ms), broad-based smooth T waves (LQT1 T-wave morphology), exercise-triggered cardiac arrest (swimming — adrenergic activation), family history (autosomal dominant, father affected). The mutation is in KCNQ1 (encodes the α-subunit of the KSQT1 channel, which carries IKs — the slow delayed rectifier K⁺ current). Loss of function → impaired repolarisation → prolonged QT → EAD-triggered TdP. Treatment priority: (1) Secondary prevention ICD — she has had an aborted SCA from confirmed VT/VF; ICD is a Class I indication regardless of medical therapy. (2) Beta-blocker (nadolol 80–160 mg OD or propranolol) — the most effective pharmacological therapy for LQT1 given the exercise/adrenergic trigger; reduces subsequent events by ~85%. (3) Genetic counselling + family screening (autosomal dominant → 50% chance in each family member). Sport absolutely contraindicated: competitive swimming. Swimming is the highest-risk sport for LQT1 (immersion + exercise → catecholamines; sudden noise of starting gun → adrenergic surge; cold water immersion → vagal + catecholamine response). Even with ICD, competitive swimming is prohibited in LQT1.

Torsades de Pointes is one of the most preventable causes of cardiac arrest. It is almost always drug-induced, almost always preceded by warning signs on the ECG, and almost always immediately reversible with magnesium. Recognising the setup before the storm is the skill this chapter teaches.

## What is Torsades de Pointes?

Torsades de Pointes ("twisting of the points") is polymorphic VT occurring in the context of a prolonged QT interval. Its hallmark ECG appearance: QRS complexes that progressively change amplitude and appear to rotate around the isoelectric baseline — tall complexes in one direction for 5–10 beats, then progressively shortening and twisting into tall complexes in the opposite direction. The rate is 150–300 bpm. TdP typically lasts 5–15 seconds then spontaneously terminates — causing a syncopal episode. If it does not terminate, it degenerates to VF.

### The mechanism

TdP is triggered by early afterdepolarisations (EADs) arising during the prolonged phase 3 repolarisation. Prolonged QT → some areas of the ventricle repolarise before others → spatial dispersion of repolarisation → a re-entrant wave propagates from a partially repolarised area to a still-refractory area → polymorphic re-entry → TdP. The first triggered beat (the EAD) occurs after a long pause (the "short-long-short" sequence: a PVC causes a compensatory pause → the next sinus beat falls on the prolonged QT → triggers TdP).

## The short-long-short initiating sequence

The sequence most often preceding TdP onset:

1. A premature beat (PVC or PAC) → creates a compensatory pause
2. The long RR interval → the next QT is even longer (the QT is inversely proportional to HR — slower rate = longer QT)
3. A beat following the long pause → falls during the T wave of the preceding beat (R-on-T phenomenon in the context of prolonged QT)
4. This triggers TdP

Clinical implication: When you see frequent PVCs in a patient with a long QT — especially if the PVCs are followed by compensatory pauses — the patient is at high risk of TdP. This is a pre-TdP warning.

## Causes of QT prolongation — the most important categories

| Category | Examples | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drugs (most common) | Class Ia antiarrhythmics (quinidine — "quinidine syncope" is TdP), class III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide), antibiotics (azithromycin, fluoroquinolones), antipsychotics (haloperidol, droperidol, chlorpromazine), antidepressants (TCAs), antiemetics (metoclopramide, high-dose ondansetron), antimalarials (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine) | hERG channel block → ↓ IKr → prolonged phase 3 |
| Electrolyte abnormalities | Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia | K⁺ gradient and Mg²⁺ stabilise ion channel kinetics; depletion → prolonged repolarisation |
| Bradycardia | Complete heart block, sinus bradycardia, post-cardioversion | QT inversely related to HR — slow HR = longer QT |
| Congenital LQTS | LQT1, LQT2, LQT3 (Chapter 11) | Loss-of-function K⁺ channel or gain-of-function late Na⁺ channel mutations |
| Structural / other | Myocarditis, ischaemia, hypothyroidism, hypothermia, intracranial haemorrhage (especially subarachnoid — massive sympathetic discharge) | Various — myocardial injury, autonomic dysregulation |

Key concept: The most dangerous combination for TdP is a QT-prolonging drug given to a hypokalaemic patient with bradycardia
Each factor independently prolongs the QT. Combined, they are synergistic: hypokalaemia reduces IKr (K⁺ ions are needed in the channel's outer vestibule to maintain open-state conductance — low extracellular K⁺ paradoxically reduces IKr outward current); bradycardia lengthens each QT cycle; the drug blocks IKr directly. The resulting QT may be critically prolonged (600–700 ms) → every beat is at risk of EAD-triggered TdP. In any patient starting a QT-prolonging drug: check QTc at baseline, check K⁺ and Mg²⁺ and correct before starting, recheck QTc 2–4 hours after the first dose or when drug reaches steady state.

## Recognition of impending TdP — the warning ECG signs

- QTc >500 ms: high risk threshold. Stop/replace QT-prolonging drugs. Avoid adding further QT-prolonging agents.
- T-wave alternans: beat-to-beat alternation in T-wave polarity or amplitude — a sign of electrical instability in the prolonged-QT ventricle
- Prominent U waves: positive deflection after the T wave in V2–V3 (especially hypokalaemia) — U waves are part of the prolonged QT complex and increase arrhythmia risk
- PVCs with short-long-short sequence: as described above

## Acute management of TdP

1. IV Magnesium sulphate 2g IV over 2–10 minutes (then 1–2 g/hour infusion)

Magnesium is the first-line emergency treatment for TdP. Mechanism: Mg²⁺ stabilises ICa,L-mediated EADs (blocks the Ca²⁺ influx that triggers EADs during phase 2/3). Works even when Mg²⁺ is normal. Terminates TdP and prevents recurrence in 80–90% of cases. Give immediately when TdP is recognised — do not wait for electrolyte results.

2. Identify and eliminate the cause

- Stop all QT-prolonging drugs
- Correct K⁺ to ≥4.5 mmol/L (supplemental K⁺ IV — higher K⁺ increases IKr → shortens QT)
- Correct Mg²⁺ to >1.0 mmol/L

3. Increase heart rate to shorten QT interval

- Temporary cardiac pacing (transvenous) at 100–110 bpm → shortens QT (QT = QTc × √RR — higher HR = shorter RR = shorter absolute QT). Pacing eliminates the long pauses that trigger TdP. Preferred over drugs if pacing is available.
- IV isoprenaline (isoproterenol) 1–4 µg/min infusion → increases HR → shortens QT. Used as bridge if temporary pacing is not immediately available. Avoid in congenital LQTS (causes catecholamine-triggered EADs in LQT1/2).

4. DC cardioversion if TdP does not spontaneously terminate (degeneration to VF).

Warning: DO NOT give additional antiarrhythmic drugs for TdP. Class Ia antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) prolong the QT further → worsen TdP. Class III drugs (amiodarone, sotalol) also prolong QT → worsen TdP. Beta-blockers in acquired TdP (bradycardia-dependent): mixed effect — reduces catecholamines (good) but slows HR further (bad). IV magnesium + pacing/isoproterenol is the correct management. The amiodarone that would treat monomorphic VT is the wrong drug for TdP.

Exam tip: Azithromycin + antimalarial combination in Indonesia — a real-world QT danger. In Indonesia, combinations including azithromycin (used for atypical pneumonia, respiratory infections) and antimalarial drugs (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine — used for malaria prophylaxis, rheumatological disease) are encountered clinically. Both prolong QT via hERG block. Their combination can dramatically prolong QT. High-risk scenario: patient with hyponatraemia, low K⁺ from diarrhoea, given azithromycin for respiratory infection, already on hydroxychloroquine for RA — this combination in a bradycardic patient is a TdP setup. Always check baseline ECG and QTc, check electrolytes, and be alert to QT-prolonging drug combinations in any patient presenting with new syncope.

Checkpoint: A 68-year-old woman with AF is started on dofetilide for rhythm control. Baseline QTc was 420 ms. On day 2, her telemetry shows QTc 540 ms and you are called for "runs of wide complex tachycardia" that self-terminate in 10–15 seconds, causing near-syncope. What is the diagnosis, what do you do in the next 5 minutes, and what do you give IV first?
This is drug-induced (acquired) Torsades de Pointes caused by dofetilide. The diagnosis is confirmed by: QTc prolonged from 420 ms to 540 ms with the QT-prolonging drug + self-terminating polymorphic VT with near-syncope. TdP classically appears on days 1–3 of dofetilide (reason dofetilide requires 3-day in-hospital initiation with continuous QTc monitoring). The next 5 minutes: (1) IV magnesium sulphate 2g over 5–10 minutes immediately — this is the first-line drug; do not wait. (2) Stop dofetilide immediately — the causative agent must be removed. (3) Check K⁺ and Mg²⁺ levels urgently — correct K⁺ to ≥4.5 mmol/L via IV supplementation (K⁺ 40 mmol in 250 mL over 1 hour). (4) Prepare temporary pacing if magnesium alone does not prevent further TdP — overdrive pacing at 100 bpm shortens QT and eliminates the pause-dependent TdP trigger. (5) Do not give amiodarone, procainamide, or any other antiarrhythmic (will worsen QT prolongation). The dofetilide should not be restarted — this patient has demonstrated susceptibility to acquired LQTS from dofetilide. AF rate control or catheter ablation for AF should be pursued instead.

sections.body:
Antiarrhythmic drugs are among the most dangerous drugs in medicine. Most suppress one arrhythmia while creating the substrate for another. The Vaughan-Williams classification organises them by mechanism — but the clinical rules about which drug is safe in which patient override simple classification every time.

## Vaughan-Williams classification

| Class | Mechanism | Effect on ECG | Key drugs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Class Ia | Moderate Na⁺ channel block (intermediate kinetics) + K⁺ channel block | ↑ QRS width + ↑ QT interval | Quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide |
| Class Ib | Weak Na⁺ channel block (fast kinetics — rapid on/off) | Minimal QRS widening; ↓ QT slightly | Lidocaine, mexiletine |
| Class Ic | Potent Na⁺ channel block (slow kinetics — slow on/off) | ↑↑ QRS width; minimal QT effect | Flecainide, propafenone |
| Class II | β-adrenergic receptor blockade → ↓ If, ↓ ICa,L in nodal tissue | ↓ HR, ↑ PR interval | Metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol, atenolol, esmolol (IV), propranolol |
| Class III | K⁺ channel block → prolonged phase 3 repolarisation | ↑↑ QT interval | Amiodarone (also I/II/IV), sotalol (also II), dofetilide, ibutilide (IV) |
| Class IV | L-type Ca²⁺ channel block → slows SA/AV nodal depolarisation | ↑ PR interval, ↓ HR | Diltiazem, verapamil (non-DHP); DHP-CCBs (nifedipine) act primarily on vascular smooth muscle |

## Class Ic drugs — the CAST trial and the structural heart disease rule

Flecainide and propafenone are highly effective at suppressing ventricular ectopy and maintaining sinus rhythm in AF. The CAST trial (Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial, 1989) was a landmark trial that changed cardiology permanently:

Post-MI patients with asymptomatic ventricular ectopy were randomised to encainide or flecainide (to suppress the PVCs) vs placebo. Result: the antiarrhythmic drugs significantly increased mortality — 3× more sudden cardiac deaths in the treated group despite successfully suppressing PVCs. The trial was stopped early.

Key concept: Class Ic drugs suppress arrhythmia markers (PVCs) while increasing the risk of fatal arrhythmias in patients with structural heart disease — the CAST lesson
The mechanism of CAST harm: Class Ic drugs are potent Na⁺ channel blockers with slow kinetics — they accumulate in the channel at fast heart rates (use-dependence). In a post-MI patient with scar, any ischaemia or tachycardia → more Na⁺ channel block → further slowing of conduction → re-entrant circuits become sustained rather than self-terminating → fatal VT/VF. The drug that suppressed 95% of PVCs (a surrogate marker) actually worsened the outcome it was meant to prevent. The CAST rule: Class Ic drugs (flecainide, propafenone) are contraindicated in: structural heart disease (ischaemic CMP, significant LVH, HF), significant coronary artery disease, valvular disease with LV dysfunction. They are safe in structurally normal hearts for SVT or AF.

## Drug-by-drug clinical profiles

### Amiodarone — the Swiss Army knife of antiarrhythmics

Amiodarone blocks all four drug classes: Na⁺ channels (Class I), β-receptors (Class II), K⁺ channels (Class III — dominant action), Ca²⁺ channels (Class IV). It is the most broadly effective antiarrhythmic drug and relatively safe in structural heart disease. However, its side-effect profile is formidable with long-term use:

- Pulmonary toxicity: interstitial pneumonitis / pulmonary fibrosis — most serious organ toxicity. Insidious onset. Monitor with annual CXR + PFTs. Risk increases with duration and dose.
- Thyroid: hypothyroidism (most common) or hyperthyroidism (either through iodine loading → excess thyroid hormone synthesis, or destructive thyroiditis). Monitor TFTs every 6 months. Contains ~37% iodine by weight — 200 mg amiodarone tablet = 75 mg iodine (WHO daily allowance = 150 µg).
- Hepatotoxicity: elevated transaminases (common, usually mild), rarely cirrhosis. Monitor LFTs.
- Corneal microdeposits: in virtually all patients on long-term amiodarone. Usually asymptomatic, rarely impair vision. Not a reason to stop.
- Photosensitivity / blue-grey skin discolouration: from iodine/amiodarone skin deposition. Use high-SPF sunscreen.
- Neuropathy, tremor, ataxia: long-term use.
- QT prolongation: amiodarone prolongs QT significantly, but despite this, TdP is paradoxically uncommon with amiodarone (<1%) compared to other QT-prolonging drugs — thought to be because amiodarone also blocks Ca²⁺ channels (reduces EAD formation) and reduces heart rate uniformly (unlike drugs that prolong QT unevenly). The QT prolongation from amiodarone is "safer" than from other class III drugs.
- Drug interactions: inhibits CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 → doubles warfarin effect (reduce warfarin dose by ~50%), increases digoxin levels, increases statin levels (myopathy risk).

IV amiodarone: 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min for 6 hours, then 0.5 mg/min for 18 hours. Always use a central line for prolonged infusions — IV amiodarone is diluted in dextrose (not saline — precipitates) and causes severe peripheral phlebitis.

### Sotalol — beta-blocker + class III

Both d- and l-isomers: d-sotalol (pure class III) + l-sotalol (β-blockade). Effective for AF maintenance and VT suppression. QT prolongation is dose-dependent and dangerous — QTc must be monitored, dose adjusted for renal function (entirely renally cleared). The d-SOTALOL trial: d-sotalol alone post-MI → increased mortality (same CAST lesson — pure K⁺ channel block increases risk in structural disease). l-sotalol's β-blockade partially offsets the proarrhythmic risk of pure class III. Still contraindicated in structural heart disease with significantly impaired EF.

### Flecainide

Most effective drug for SVT (AVNRT, AVRT), AF maintenance, and CPVT (direct RyR2 block). Structurally normal hearts only (CAST rule). Useful as "pill in the pocket" for SVT (200–300 mg PO at onset — patient carries the tablet and takes only during tachycardia episodes). Increases the defibrillation threshold (relevant if patient has ICD — discuss with EP). Increases flutter rate paradoxically but can cause 1:1 AV conduction of flutter (see below).

Warning: Flecainide for AF can convert AF to atrial flutter and then conduct 1:1 at high ventricular rates. Flecainide slows the atrial flutter rate (from ~300 to ~200 bpm), making 1:1 AV conduction physiologically possible (the AV node can keep up at 200 bpm). This produces a wide complex tachycardia at ~200 bpm (LBBB aberrancy from rapid rate) that is haemodynamically catastrophic. Solution: always add a rate-limiting agent (beta-blocker or non-DHP CCB) when using flecainide for AF in patients at risk of flutter conversion. The combination: flecainide (rhythm control) + metoprolol (AV nodal protection) is standard practice.

### Beta-blockers (Class II)

The safest antiarrhythmic class for almost every context. Reduce automaticity, slow AV conduction, raise VF threshold. First-line for: rate control in AF (especially with HFrEF), prevention of SVT recurrence, post-MI arrhythmia suppression, LQTS (LQT1, LQT2), CPVT, appropriate ICD shock reduction. Avoid in: high-degree AV block (without pacemaker), severe asthma (relative), decompensated HF (do not start acutely — see HF guide).

### Digoxin

Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase inhibitor → ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → NCX reversal → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺ → positive inotropy + enhanced vagal tone → slows AV node. Rate control in AF (especially at rest — poor rate control with exercise). Narrow therapeutic window (target 0.5–0.9 ng/mL). Toxicity: nausea/vomiting (early), visual disturbances (yellow-green haloes), bradycardia/AV block/bidirectional VT (late). Toxic at lower levels in: elderly, hypokalaemia (K⁺ competes with digoxin for Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase binding — low K⁺ → more digoxin binding → toxicity at lower serum levels), renal impairment, hypothyroidism.

Exam tip: The proarrhythmia hierarchy — which drugs cause which arrhythmias: Class Ia (quinidine, procainamide): TdP (QT prolongation) + widen QRS at fast rates
Class Ic (flecainide): flutter with 1:1 conduction; fatal VT in structural disease (CAST)
Class III (sotalol, dofetilide): TdP (most proarrhythmic for TdP among class III after quinidine)
Amiodarone: TdP risk lowest among class III; pulmonary/thyroid/hepatic toxicity
Digoxin: bidirectional VT (CPVT-like appearance); PAT with block; AV block
Adenosine: transient AF induction (in ~12% of patients — usually self-terminating); dangerous in WPW

Checkpoint: A cardiologist wants to start flecainide 100 mg BD for paroxysmal AF in a 58-year-old man. His echo: EF 52%, mild concentric LVH (IVS 13 mm), no wall motion abnormality. His exercise ECG shows no ischaemia. Is flecainide safe here, and what additional precaution must you add if you proceed?
This is a borderline situation. Flecainide is contraindicated in: (1) ischaemic CMP — exercise ECG shows no ischaemia, so this concern is addressed; (2) significant LVH — the IVS of 13 mm represents mild-moderate LVH. ESC guidelines consider significant LVH (IVS ≥14 mm by convention in some guidelines) a relative contraindication to class Ic drugs. At 13 mm this is borderline — many centres would still use flecainide with caution; others would prefer propafenone, sotalol, or dronedarone as safer alternatives for AF with LVH. If proceeding with flecainide: essential additional precaution — add a rate-limiting drug (metoprolol 25–50 mg OD or bisoprolol 2.5 mg OD). This prevents the risk of flecainide converting AF to atrial flutter with 1:1 AV conduction. Monitor QRS width (if QRS widens >25% from baseline on flecainide → drug toxicity/accumulation → reduce dose or stop). Inform the patient about "pill-in-the-pocket" dosing versus continuous use — for infrequent AF episodes, pill-in-the-pocket (200–300 mg PO at onset) may be preferred over daily dosing to reduce cumulative exposure.

sections.body:
Catheter ablation has transformed arrhythmia management from drug dependence to cure. Understanding the principles of mapping, the targets for each arrhythmia, and the device selection rules gives you the framework to know when to refer — and what to expect.

## Principles of catheter ablation

Catheter ablation delivers energy to a precisely targeted region of cardiac tissue to create a lesion — a permanent scar that electrically isolates the target (ablation of a focus) or interrupts a circuit (ablation of a critical isthmus). Modern ablation uses:

- Radiofrequency (RF) ablation: alternating current (350–500 kHz) delivered to the tip of a catheter → resistive heating of tissue → coagulation necrosis. Point-by-point or continuous drag technique. Contact force sensing (open-irrigation catheters) improves lesion quality.
- Cryoablation: liquid nitrogen or nitrous oxide delivered to the catheter tip → tissue freezing → ice crystal formation → cell death. Used primarily for PV isolation in AF (cryoballoon catheter — balloon inflates at PV ostium, cryoenergy delivered circumferentially). Advantage over RF: lower risk of inadvertent damage to oesophagus and no risk of char formation.
- Pulsed-field ablation (PFA): newest modality — delivers ultra-short, high-voltage electrical pulses → irreversible electroporation of cell membranes → cell death without thermal injury. Highly selective for cardiac myocytes (vs thermal modalities which can affect adjacent structures). Emerging standard for AF ablation — faster procedure, lower oesophageal fistula risk.

## Electroanatomical mapping

Modern EP labs use 3D electroanatomical mapping systems (CARTO, EnSite) that combine catheter position (tracked magnetically or electrically in 3D space) with local electrogram recordings. The mapping system builds a 3D model of the cardiac chamber with:

- Voltage mapping: identifies scar (low-voltage areas, <0.5 mV) and healthy myocardium (>1.5 mV) → critical for VT ablation (scar boundary is where the VT circuit lives)
- Activation mapping: colour-coded display of when each point is activated relative to a reference → identifies the earliest activation site (focus in AT, automatic tachycardia) or the critical isthmus (re-entry)
- Pace-mapping: pacing from catheter tip and comparing the 12-lead QRS morphology to the clinical arrhythmia → 12/12 pace-map match = catheter is at or near the origin of the arrhythmia

## Ablation by arrhythmia — targets and outcomes

| Arrhythmia | Ablation target | Success rate | Key complications |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AVNRT | Slow pathway (posteroinferior AV node region) | >98% single procedure | AV block requiring pacemaker <1% |
| AVRT (accessory pathway) | Accessory pathway location on the AV annulus | 95%+ (left free-wall highest) | AV block (parahisian paths 3–5%); cardiac tamponade <1% |
| Typical atrial flutter | Cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) | 95%+ single procedure | Very rare; tamponade <0.5% |
| Focal AT | AT focus (identified by activation/pace-map) | 85–90% right atrial; 80% left atrial | Tamponade, phrenic nerve injury |
| Paroxysmal AF | Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) | 70–80% single procedure; 85%+ after 2+ procedures | LA-oesophageal fistula <0.1%; PV stenosis 1–2%; stroke 1–2%; tamponade 1% |
| Persistent/LS persistent AF | PVI ± posterior wall isolation ± substrate modification | 40–60% single procedure | Same as above; higher recurrence rates |
| Monomorphic VT (scar-related) | Critical isthmus within scar (identified by voltage/activation mapping) | 60–80% at 1 year; VT storm responds acutely ~90% | Tamponade; AV block (if near conduction system); haemodynamic compromise during VT mapping |
| RVOT-VT (idiopathic) | RVOT focus | >90% single procedure | Rare |
| CTI ablation for flutter after cardiac surgery | Cavotricuspid isthmus or incisional circuit | Lower than typical flutter (scar-related circuits) | Higher complication rate post-surgery |

## Pacemaker systems — modes and selection

Pacemaker nomenclature (NBG code — first three letters are most important):

- First letter: chamber paced (A = atrium, V = ventricle, D = dual)
- Second letter: chamber sensed (A, V, D, O = none)
- Third letter: response to sensing (I = inhibited, T = triggered, D = dual, R = rate-responsive in 4th position)

| Mode | Meaning | When used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| VVI(R) | Paces and senses ventricle; inhibited by sensed beat. Rate-responsive if R. | Permanent AF with bradycardia (no atrial activity to track). Simple, reliable. Loses AV synchrony. |
| AAI(R) | Paces and senses atrium only; inhibited by sensed atrial beat. | Sinus node dysfunction with intact AV conduction. Preserves AV synchrony. Not if AV block present. |
| DDD(R) | Paces and senses both chambers; tracks atrial rate to drive ventricular pacing. Dual response. | AV block with normal sinus node. The most physiological mode — AV synchrony preserved. "Dual chamber pacing." |
| DDI(R) | Dual chamber pacing and sensing; inhibited response (does not track atrial rate). | Tachy-brady syndrome — prevents tracking of fast atrial rates to the ventricle while still providing bradycardia support. |

## ICD — tiered therapy

Modern ICDs deliver three tiers of therapy for detected ventricular arrhythmia:

1. Antitachycardia pacing (ATP): burst or ramp pacing at a rate faster than the VT → enters the VT circuit → terminates the re-entry without a shock. Successful in 70–90% of slow VT (<200 bpm). Painless. First-line therapy for detected VT in the "VT zone."
2. Synchronised cardioversion (low-energy shock): for VT that ATP failed to terminate. Painful but lower energy than defibrillation.
3. Defibrillation (high-energy shock): for VF or very fast VT. 35–40 J biphasic (monophasic devices: 200–360 J). Painful — patients describe it as being hit in the chest.

Subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD): the sensing and shocking lead is entirely subcutaneous (no intravascular component) — placed along the left lateral chest wall. Advantages: no vascular access complications, no lead-endocarditis risk, easily removed. Disadvantages: no ATP capability (cannot pace-terminate VT — only shock), no pacing for bradycardia, larger generator. Preferred in: young patients (long life expectancy, avoid endovascular lead complications), patients with vascular access problems or prior lead infection, congenital heart disease with complex anatomy.

Exam tip: Inappropriate ICD shocks — the most common cause is AF with rapid ventricular rate detected as VF. An ICD "sees" a fast ventricular rate and delivers a shock. If the fast rate is AF rather than VF, the shock is inappropriate. Consequences: pain (patient trauma), proarrhythmic (shock can trigger VF in some patients), battery depletion. Prevention: (1) AF detection algorithms in modern ICDs discriminate AF from VF by onset and regularity; (2) adequate AF rate control reduces the risk of ventricular rate exceeding the VF detection threshold; (3) dual-chamber ICD (with atrial lead) can detect atrial activity and identify AF vs VF by comparing atrial and ventricular rates. Any patient who receives an ICD shock should have the device interrogated — appropriate vs inappropriate must be determined.

Checkpoint: A 55-year-old with ischaemic CMP (EF 28%) and CRT-D has his device interrogated. The printout shows: ATP delivery at onset of 175 bpm VT → successfully terminates after 8 paced beats → no shock delivered. His wife asks why the device "did nothing" when he felt dizzy. How do you explain what actually happened?
The device worked perfectly — it detected VT at 175 bpm and delivered antitachycardia pacing (ATP), which terminated the VT in 8 beats without a shock. Explain to the wife: (1) The ICD is not just a "shock box" — modern ICDs deliver tiered therapy. For a relatively slow VT (175 bpm), the device first tries rapid pacing bursts (ATP) to break the re-entry circuit. ATP is painless and works in ~80% of slower VTs. (2) The dizziness her husband felt was from the brief VT episode itself (a few seconds of VT → reduced cardiac output → presyncope) — completely normal. The device terminated it before it could become a sustained dangerous arrhythmia. (3) If ATP had failed, the device would have escalated to a cardioversion shock, then a full defibrillation shock. The hierarchy of therapy is designed to use the least uncomfortable and energy-consuming intervention first. (4) This event should be reported to his EP team — recurrent VT on optimal GDMT may warrant VT ablation (see Chapter 8) or medication adjustment. The fact that ATP terminated it successfully means it was monomorphic re-entrant VT (ATP cannot terminate VF).

Arrhythmia medicine has a set of recognition patterns that every clinician must own instantly — because the cost of a 30-second delay in recognition is sometimes death. This chapter consolidates the entire guide into the patterns that matter most under pressure.

## Pattern 1 — The irregular wide complex tachycardia with bizarre morphology

This is the most dangerous single ECG pattern in arrhythmia medicine. Irregular + wide + bizarre = AF with WPW until proven otherwise. Every other irregular tachycardia (AF with aberrancy, polymorphic VT) either has different clinical context or a different ECG appearance. The distinguishing feature: in AF+WPW, the QRS morphologies continuously change beat-to-beat (varying degrees of fusion between AP-conducted and AV node-conducted beats) and some beats are very wide (maximally pre-excited) while others are narrower. Rate is typically 200–300 bpm.

Red flag action: If the patient is haemodynamically unstable → immediate DC cardioversion. If stable → IV procainamide. Never adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, or digoxin.

## Pattern 2 — The pause-terminated tachycardia with syncope

Tachycardia → abrupt termination → long pause → syncope → sinus restart. This is the Holter pattern of tachy-brady syndrome. Every other cause of syncope in a tachycardia patient (haemodynamic: low BP during fast rate) resolves when the tachycardia terminates — this patient collapses at the exact moment the tachycardia stops. Recognised on: Holter monitor, cardiac event monitor, ILR recording.

Red flag action: Do not treat the tachycardia first (drugs that control AF will worsen the bradycardic pause). Implant pacemaker first, then address the tachyarrhythmia.

## Pattern 3 — The "flutter in disguise" at 150 bpm

Regular tachycardia, ventricular rate exactly 150 bpm, narrow or wide QRS, apparent "flat" baseline between QRS. You have to actively look for the flutter waves — they are there, but one is buried in the QRS and one is visible between QRS complexes. The baseline is never truly flat in flutter — there is always a subtle sawtooth.

Red flag action: Give adenosine as a diagnostic manoeuvre (will increase AV block → ventricular rate halves → flutter waves unmask). Do not cardiovert first without at least attempting diagnosis — knowing it is flutter changes the long-term plan (CTI ablation, not just rhythm control).

## Pattern 4 — The long QT patient on multiple drugs who develops syncope

Any patient on QT-prolonging drugs who develops syncope or near-syncope should be assumed to have TdP until an ECG or rhythm strip proves otherwise. The common scenario: elderly woman on azithromycin (respiratory infection) + metoclopramide (nausea) + prior thiazide diuretic (hypokalaemia) → QTc now 570 ms → TdP → syncope labelled "vasovagal."

Red flag action: Obtain an ECG immediately and measure QTc. Check electrolytes. If QTc >500 ms → stop all QT-prolonging drugs, correct K⁺ to ≥4.5 and Mg²⁺, give IV Mg²⁺ 2g if TdP suspected. Continuous telemetry.

## The 12 most dangerous arrhythmia drug errors — a synthesis table

| # | Error | Why it kills |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Verapamil for wide complex tachycardia (presumed SVT) | If WCT is VT → vasodilation + negative inotropy → haemodynamic collapse in patient already compensating with high SVR |
| 2 | Adenosine in AF + WPW | Blocks AV node → all AF conduction via AP → ventricular rate 250–300+ bpm → VF |
| 3 | Flecainide in ischaemic CMP or significant LVH | CAST — drug-facilitated fatal VT. Na⁺ channel block slows conduction in scars → sustained lethal re-entry |
| 4 | Adding a second QT-prolonging drug to a patient already on one | Additive QTc prolongation → TdP. Especially dangerous: azithromycin + antipsychotic; fluoroquinolone + sotalol |
| 5 | Treating symptomatic Mobitz II without pacing | Mobitz II can progress to complete heart block without warning; ventricular escape is unreliable (20–40 bpm) → syncope, cardiac arrest |
| 6 | Starting flecainide for AF without adding a rate-limiting agent | Flecainide slows flutter to ~200 bpm → 1:1 AV conduction → wide complex tachycardia at 200 bpm → haemodynamic collapse |
| 7 | Giving digoxin or diltiazem for rate control in AF + WPW | Both enhance AP conduction by blocking AV node → rapidly pre-excited AF → VF (same mechanism as adenosine) |
| 8 | Amiodarone IV infusion via peripheral line without dilution | Amiodarone in peripheral veins → severe phlebitis, thrombophlebitis, tissue necrosis. Use central line or dilute significantly |
| 9 | Giving sodium channel blocker (flecainide) to a Brugada patient | Na⁺ channel block → unmasks/worsens Brugada pattern → may precipitate VF. Na⁺ channel blockers are the diagnostic provocation test in Brugada — they unmask it because they worsen it. |
| 10 | Not checking QTc before discharge on a new QT-prolonging drug | Drug-induced QT prolongation may not manifest for 24–72h (accumulation to steady state). A 12-lead ECG 2–4h after the first dose or on day 2 of the new drug is mandatory for high-risk drugs. |
| 11 | Isoproterenol in congenital LQTS (LQT1/2) with TdP | Isoproterenol increases catecholamines → triggers EADs in LQT1/2 (adrenergic-triggered) → worsens TdP. Use pacing instead in congenital LQTS. Isoproterenol is appropriate only for acquired (drug-induced, pause-dependent) TdP. |
| 12 | Cardioverting MAT (multifocal AT) | MAT is an automatic tachycardia from multiple foci driven by metabolic abnormality. Cardioversion terminates re-entry — it does nothing to automatic foci. MAT restarts immediately after the shock. Treat the metabolic cause instead. |

## Red flag ECG findings requiring immediate action

Alert: Act within minutes on these findings:
• QTc >600 ms in a monitored patient → immediate telemetry review, check for T-wave alternans, stop all QT-prolonging drugs, give IV Mg²⁺
• Complete heart block + HR <30 bpm or haemodynamic compromise → temporary pacing NOW; atropine as bridge
• Irregular wide complex tachycardia >200 bpm with bizarre QRS → assume AF+WPW, prepare for cardioversion, give procainamide if stable
• Short PR + delta waves in a patient with syncope or palpitations → EP referral, risk stratification, do not discharge without risk assessment
• Regular narrow complex tachycardia 150 bpm not responding to adenosine → think flutter with 2:1, think AT — do not give amiodarone (it prolongs QT and may not help)
• Monomorphic wide complex tachycardia in a patient with known CMP → VT until proven otherwise → amiodarone or cardioversion; never verapamil

Checkpoint: In a single clinical scenario: a 70-year-old woman with known AF and HFrEF (EF 30%) is admitted with diarrhoea and vomiting for 48 hours. She is on digoxin 250 µg OD, furosemide, bisoprolol, sacubitril/valsartan. On admission: HR 115 bpm irregular, K⁺ 2.7 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ 0.5 mmol/L, creatinine 160 µmol/L (baseline 100). ECG: AF with rapid ventricular rate, QTc 540 ms, occasional PVCs with short-long-short sequences on the monitor strip. What are the three most important immediate actions and why?
1. IV potassium and magnesium replacement — immediately and urgently. K⁺ 2.7 mmol/L + Mg²⁺ 0.5 mmol/L = critically depleted. This combination: (a) prolongs QT further (K⁺ depletion reduces IKr; Mg²⁺ depletion destabilises Ca²⁺ handling → more EAD formation); (b) dramatically potentiates digoxin toxicity (low K⁺ competes less with digoxin for Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase → more digoxin binding → toxicity at a serum level that was therapeutic when K⁺ was normal). IV potassium chloride 40 mmol over 1–2 hours via cardiac monitoring. IV magnesium sulphate 2–4g over 20 minutes. Target K⁺ ≥4.5 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ ≥0.8 mmol/L. 2. Hold digoxin and check digoxin level immediately. She has: acute renal injury (creatinine 160 from baseline 100 — AKI from vomiting-induced dehydration → reduced digoxin clearance → accumulation), low K⁺ (potentiates digoxin toxicity), and a QTc of 540 ms with PVCs suggesting digoxin toxicity pattern. Digoxin level must be drawn. Until the level and AKI resolve, withhold digoxin entirely. The short-long-short PVC sequences + QTc 540 ms = this patient is one step away from TdP or digoxin-triggered bidirectional VT. 3. Continuous cardiac monitoring and telemetry — alert nursing staff to call immediately for any sustained wide complex tachycardia or TdP. IV Mg²⁺ 2g already given as both treatment and prevention (for TdP). Do not give additional QT-prolonging drugs for rate control (amiodarone would worsen this). Bisoprolol can help rate control if haemodynamically tolerated (check BP first — sacubitril/valsartan + dehydration + AKI → BP may be low). Hold furosemide until volume status clarified (dehydrated from D&V). Recheck ECG after electrolyte correction.

sections.body:
Arrhythmia questions test drug contraindications, mechanism recognition, and treatment selection under time pressure. The same systematic approach — identify the arrhythmia type, identify the contraindication, answer the actual question asked — works every time.

## The arrhythmia MCQ framework — five questions before answering

1. Bradycardia or tachycardia? If bradycardia — is it symptomatic? Does it need pacing? If tachycardia — narrow or wide?
2. Narrow complex tachycardia: what mechanism? Regular narrow → SVT type (AVNRT vs AVRT vs AT vs flutter). Irregular narrow → AF or MAT. Regular exactly 150 → think flutter.
3. Wide complex tachycardia: VT or SVT with aberrancy or pre-excited? Assume VT in structural heart disease. Check for AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, extreme axis.
4. Is there a structural heart disease context? EF <40% → no flecainide, no verapamil for VT. WPW → no AV nodal blockers in wide complex. Post-MI → 40-day ICD rule.
5. What is the question asking? Acute management vs long-term vs mechanism vs contraindication vs ablation target vs device selection.

## The arrhythmia trap library — 14 high-yield traps

| # | Scenario signal | Trap answer | Why wrong / correct answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Wide complex tachycardia, rate 200 bpm, patient with prior MI and EF 30% | "Give IV verapamil — may be SVT with aberrancy" | Verapamil in VT causes haemodynamic collapse. Treat as VT: IV amiodarone or cardiovert. The prior MI + EF 30% context makes VT ~95% likely. |
| 2 | Regular tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm; adenosine slows ventricular rate temporarily then tachycardia resumes | "Adenosine terminated the tachycardia — was AVNRT" | Adenosine revealed atrial flutter by temporarily increasing AV block (rate halved) but the tachycardia resumed when AV nodal block resolved. Continuation = flutter (or AT), not AVNRT. AVNRT terminates completely and does not resume. |
| 3 | Irregular rapid wide complex tachycardia, rate 250 bpm, QRS morphology continuously changes | "Give adenosine or diltiazem for AF" | This is AF + WPW. AV nodal blockers enhance AP conduction → VF. Cardiovert (unstable) or procainamide (stable). Never adenosine/verapamil/diltiazem/digoxin. |
| 4 | Post-MI patient 3 weeks ago, EF 28%, frequent PVCs on Holter | "Start flecainide to suppress PVCs — reduces SCD risk" | CAST: flecainide in post-MI structural disease increases SCD 3×. PVC suppression is a surrogate marker — it does not predict outcome and flecainide kills. Plan: reassess EF at 3 months of GDMT; if EF remains ≤35% → primary prevention ICD. |
| 5 | Symptomatic Mobitz II, no syncope yet, QRS 140 ms LBBB morphology | "Observe — asymptomatic, doesn't need pacing yet" | Mobitz II requires permanent pacing even when asymptomatic (Class I). The wide QRS confirms infranodal disease; progression to complete heart block can be sudden and fatal. Pace now. |
| 6 | AVNRT terminating with adenosine; patient wants definitive treatment | "Long-term beta-blockers — curative" | Beta-blockers control but do not cure AVNRT. Curative treatment: slow pathway ablation (>98% success, <1% AV block risk). This is the correct answer for "definitive" or "curative" treatment. |
| 7 | Asymptomatic WPW pattern on routine ECG in a 30-year-old | "No treatment needed — asymptomatic" | Risk stratification is required. If AP has a short refractory period (<250 ms) → high risk of VF during AF → AP ablation recommended. Non-invasive (exercise test — abrupt loss of delta waves = reassuring) or invasive (EP study) risk stratification is indicated before dismissal. |
| 8 | 20-year-old swimmer, QTc 520 ms, broad-based T waves, collapses during race | "Start sotalol for arrhythmia suppression" | LQT1 (exercise/swimming trigger, broad-based T waves). Sotalol prolongs QT further (class III) and would worsen TdP risk. Treatment: beta-blockers (nadolol) + ICD (aborted SCA = secondary prevention). Sotalol is contraindicated in LQTS. |
| 9 | Rapid irregular tachycardia, COPD patient, ≥3 P-wave morphologies visible | "Cardiovert for AF" | MAT — cardioversion does nothing for automatic foci. Treat COPD exacerbation, correct electrolytes, consider verapamil for rate control. Not cardioversion. |
| 10 | Brugada pattern on ECG + syncope + right precordial ST elevation (coved type) | "Start flecainide to prevent arrhythmia" | Flecainide is a Na⁺ channel blocker — the exact type of drug used to unmask (and worsen) Brugada syndrome. It is absolutely contraindicated. Treatment: ICD + quinidine (if needed). Flecainide could precipitate fatal VF. |
| 11 | Acquired TdP from sotalol, QTc 560 ms, short-long-short initiating sequence | "Give amiodarone for polymorphic VT" | Amiodarone prolongs QT (class III) → worsens the mechanism of TdP. Give IV Mg²⁺ + stop sotalol + correct electrolytes + consider overdrive pacing. Amiodarone is the wrong drug for TdP. |
| 12 | Tachy-brady syndrome on Holter; cardiologist prescribes flecainide before pacemaker | "Correct — flecainide controls the AF component" | Flecainide will suppress AF but prolongs the sinus pause after AF termination (drug-enhanced SA node suppression). The dangerous pause gets longer. Pacemaker first, then antiarrhythmic therapy for the AF component. |
| 13 | VT storm — 5 episodes of VT in 24 hours, ICD delivering multiple shocks | "Increase ICD sensitivity settings" | VT storm management: deep sedation (reduces sympathetic drive), IV beta-blocker (esmolol), IV amiodarone, urgent VT ablation. Increasing ICD sensitivity does not address the underlying VT generation. |
| 14 | AF in a 65-year-old woman with HTN and DM. GP prescribed aspirin 100 mg for stroke prevention. | "Aspirin is appropriate for lone AF" | CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 3 (H + A [65–74] + D + Sc [female]). Anticoagulation (DOAC) mandatory at score ≥3 in women. Aspirin provides <22% stroke risk reduction vs DOAC's 60–70%, with equivalent or greater bleeding risk. Aspirin is not guideline-recommended for AF stroke prevention. |

## High-yield synthesis vignette — the complete arrhythmia patient

Checkpoint: A 48-year-old man with no known cardiac disease presents to A&E. He reports 2-hour history of palpitations and mild dizziness. HR 195 bpm, BP 108/70, SpO₂ 98%. ECG: regular narrow complex tachycardia at 195 bpm. P waves not clearly visible in standard leads; in V1 there is a small positive deflection immediately after the QRS (pseudo-R' pattern). Modified Valsalva manoeuvre: tachycardia abruptly terminates. Post-conversion sinus ECG: short PR interval 118 ms, delta waves visible in V1–V5, wide QRS 130 ms. He asks whether he can take up competitive swimming.
Initial diagnosis: Orthodromic AVRT (WPW) or AVNRT. The pseudo-R' in V1 after the QRS and abrupt termination with Valsalva are consistent with AVNRT (retrograde P buried at end of QRS, RP <70 ms). However, the post-conversion ECG changes everything. Post-conversion ECG reveals WPW pattern: short PR (118 ms), delta waves, wide QRS = pre-excitation. This was orthodromic AVRT (not AVNRT) — the accessory pathway conducted retrogradely, producing a short RP tachycardia that looked like AVNRT. The delta waves were absent during tachycardia (normal QRS during orthodromic AVRT — activated via AV node anterograde) but now visible in sinus rhythm. This distinction matters for management. Acute management was correct: Valsalva was safe and appropriate for narrow complex AVRT. Adenosine would also have been safe here (orthodromic AVRT = narrow QRS = conduction via AV node anterograde = AV nodal block terminates the circuit safely). Definitive management: Electrophysiology study and accessory pathway ablation. Success rate 95%+. Given confirmed WPW syndrome (symptomatic — tachycardia occurred), ablation is the standard recommendation. On competitive swimming: Competitive swimming cannot be cleared until risk stratification of the AP is complete. Before ablation: the AP refractory period must be measured (EP study). If AP refractory period <250 ms → high risk of dangerous AF with rapid pre-excited conduction → competitive sport contraindicated until AP ablated. If AP refractory period >250 ms and exercise test shows abrupt loss of pre-excitation → lower risk, but most guidelines still recommend ablation before clearance for competitive sport. After successful ablation: full clearance for competitive swimming (including high-intensity competitive sport). The WPW is cured — no residual risk. Immediate discharge instructions: Do not participate in competitive sport until EP review and ablation. If palpitations recur: attend A&E and request an ECG during palpitations. Take no medications without informing the treating physician (some drugs worsen WPW). Urgent outpatient EP referral.

## The final arrhythmia exam checklist

Alert: Before every arrhythmia answer — verify:
✓ Wide complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise — never verapamil
✓ WPW with AF or wide complex = no AV nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, beta-blockers in pre-excited AF)
✓ Flecainide/propafenone = structural heart disease contraindication (CAST rule)
✓ TdP = IV Mg²⁺ first; no amiodarone; stop QT-prolonging drugs; correct K⁺/Mg²⁺
✓ Mobitz II = permanent pacemaker even if asymptomatic (Class I)
✓ Tachy-brady syndrome = pacemaker first, then treat tachyarrhythmia
✓ Typical flutter at 150 bpm = CTI ablation is curative (>95%)
✓ AVNRT/AVRT cure = ablation (not drugs); adenosine safe in narrow AVRT; dangerous in WPW
✓ LQT1 = beta-blockers (exercise trigger); LQT3 = mexiletine (late Na⁺ current)
✓ Brugada = no Na⁺ channel blockers; quinidine + ICD
✓ CPVT = nadolol + flecainide; no competitive sport
✓ AF stroke prevention = DOAC (not aspirin); CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 male / ≥3 female → anticoagulate
✓ Cardioversion for AF >48h unknown duration = TOE first or 3 weeks anticoagulation before
✓ MAT = treat the cause (COPD, electrolytes); no cardioversion
✓ Post-cardiac arrest with STEMI = immediate coronary angiography ± PCI

sections.body:
Every arrhythmia arises from one of three mechanisms: abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or re-entry. Identifying the mechanism from the ECG tells you which drugs will work and which will not.

## Three mechanisms — one framework

### Mechanism 1 — Abnormal automaticity

Any cardiac cell can depolarise spontaneously if its resting membrane potential is abnormally elevated (less negative) — from ischaemia, hypokalaemia, catecholamine excess, or drug toxicity. These "enhanced" automatic foci fire faster than the SA node and suppress it (or fire from lower in the system when the SA node is sick).

- Normal automaticity: SA node > AV node > Purkinje fibres — higher levels suppress lower ones (overdrive suppression via the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase — faster pacing drives more Na⁺ into the cell → Na⁺/K⁺ pump upregulates → hyperpolarises the cell → suppresses spontaneous depolarisation in subsidiary pacemakers)
- Enhanced automaticity: metabolic changes raise the resting potential of a subsidiary pacemaker cell → faster phase 4 depolarisation → fires before SA node. Causes: ischaemia, digitalis toxicity, catecholamines, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia. Examples: junctional tachycardia (accelerated junctional rhythm), focal atrial tachycardia, parasystole, accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR post-MI)
- Overdrive suppression is lost in enhanced automaticity (unlike normal automaticity) — fast pacing does not suppress the focus

### Mechanism 2 — Triggered activity

Triggered arrhythmias are initiated by afterdepolarisations — membrane voltage oscillations that occur after an action potential and can reach threshold to trigger a new action potential.

Early afterdepolarisations (EADs): Occur during phase 2 or 3 (during the plateau or early repolarisation). Mechanism: prolonged action potential duration → reactivation of L-type Ca²⁺ channels or late Na⁺ current → oscillation → EAD → triggered beat. Conditions that prolong the AP: hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia (long RR intervals allow more Ca²⁺ accumulation), QT-prolonging drugs. The arrhythmia: Torsades de Pointes — the classic EAD-triggered arrhythmia. Responds to: Mg²⁺ (IV), pacing or isoproterenol to shorten QT, eliminate QT-prolonging drugs.

Delayed afterdepolarisations (DADs): Occur in phase 4, after full repolarisation. Mechanism: Ca²⁺ overload in the sarcoplasmic reticulum → spontaneous Ca²⁺ release → activates Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCX) → net inward current → DAD → triggered beat. Conditions: digoxin toxicity (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase block → Na⁺ rise → NCX reversal → Ca²⁺ overload), catecholamine excess, heart failure (Ca²⁺ cycling abnormalities), CPVT (RyR2 mutation → spontaneous SR Ca²⁺ release). Responds to: beta-blockers (reduce Ca²⁺ loading), verapamil (reduces Ca²⁺ entry), adenosine (in CPVT — suppresses cAMP-mediated DAD).

### Mechanism 3 — Re-entry (the most common mechanism)

Re-entry accounts for the majority of clinically important tachycardias (AF, flutter, AVNRT, AVRT, monomorphic VT, most SVTs). Three conditions are required for re-entry:

1. Two electrically distinct conduction pathways with different properties
2. Unidirectional block in one pathway — a premature impulse finds one pathway refractory (blocks) and conducts only through the other
3. Sufficient conduction time — the impulse travelling the long way around the circuit must arrive after the fast pathway has recovered from refractoriness

Key concept: Re-entry is an electrical circus — a wavefront chasing its own tail through a fixed or functional circuit
Imagine two bridges between the same two towns: Bridge A (fast conduction, long refractory period) and Bridge B (slow conduction, short refractory period). A premature impulse arrives early. Bridge A is still refractory (it just conducted the last beat) — blocks. Bridge B is recovered — conducts slowly. By the time the impulse arrives at the far end of Bridge B, Bridge A has recovered — conducts retrogradely. Now the impulse is going in a circle: forward through B, retrograde through A, forward through B again... This is AVNRT in essence. Drugs that interrupt re-entry work by prolonging the refractory period of one limb (so the circulating impulse meets refractory tissue) or by slowing conduction enough to cause conduction block (the impulse can't make it around the circuit fast enough).

## Classification framework — approach every arrhythmia with this

Before identifying a specific arrhythmia, answer these questions in order:

1. Rate: <60 bpm (bradycardia), 60–100 (normal), >100 (tachycardia)
2. QRS width: narrow (<120 ms) or wide (≥120 ms). Narrow QRS = ventricular activation via the normal His-Purkinje system. Wide QRS = aberrant conduction (BBB), accessory pathway, or ventricular origin (VT).
3. Regularity: regular (fixed RR intervals) or irregular. Irregular tachycardias: AF (irregularly irregular), multifocal AT, AF with varying BBB.
4. P wave morphology and relationship to QRS: Are P waves present? Positive or negative? Before or after QRS? PR interval — short/long/variable?
5. Response to vagal manoeuvres / adenosine: Terminates → nodal re-entry (AVNRT, AVRT). Slows but does not terminate → atrial tachycardia or flutter (reveals atrial activity). No effect → VT.

## Broad classification

| Category | Mechanism | Key ECG features | Classic examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sinus node dysfunction | Abnormal automaticity (decreased) / exit block | Absent or slow P waves; long sinus pauses | Sick sinus syndrome, sinus pause, sinus bradycardia |
| AV block | Conduction delay or block at AV node or infranodal level | Prolonged PR, dropped QRS, AV dissociation | 1°, 2° Mobitz I/II, 3° (complete) AV block |
| SVT — re-entrant | Re-entry using AV node (AVNRT, AVRT) or atrial circuit (flutter) | Narrow QRS, regular, 150–250 bpm, P often buried | AVNRT, AVRT, typical atrial flutter |
| SVT — focal | Enhanced automaticity or triggered activity in the atrium | Abnormal P wave morphology, may be warm-up onset | Focal atrial tachycardia, junctional tachycardia |
| Atrial fibrillation | Multiple re-entrant wavelets + focal triggers (PV triggers) | Irregularly irregular, no organised P waves, undulating baseline | AF — paroxysmal, persistent, long-standing persistent |
| VT — re-entrant | Re-entry around scar or bundle branches | Wide QRS, monomorphic or polymorphic, AV dissociation | Monomorphic VT (scar-related), RVOT-VT, Bundle branch re-entry VT |
| VF | Multiple disorganised re-entrant wavelets | Chaotic, no organised QRS, no cardiac output | Primary VF, VF from degenerated VT |
| Triggered | EADs or DADs | QT prolongation → TdP; digoxin toxicity patterns | Torsades de Pointes, digoxin toxicity (bidirectional VT in CPVT) |

Checkpoint: On the monitor: regular tachycardia at 175 bpm, QRS 0.10 s (narrow), P waves not clearly visible. A Valsalva manoeuvre abruptly terminates the arrhythmia to sinus rhythm. What mechanism does this confirm, what arrhythmia is most likely, and what does "abrupt termination" tell you about the mechanism (vs gradual slowing)?
Re-entrant tachycardia using the AV node — specifically AVNRT (AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia) is the most likely diagnosis. The Valsalva manoeuvre increases vagal tone → transiently slows AV nodal conduction → if the conduction velocity in one limb of the re-entrant circuit drops enough, the circulating wavefront meets refractory tissue → circuit breaks → tachycardia terminates abruptly. "Abrupt termination" vs "gradual slowing": this distinction is one of the most important in arrhythmia diagnosis. Abrupt termination (P-QRS-P-QRS-P-QRS → sudden sinus P → done) indicates re-entrant tachycardia — the circuit is broken in one beat. Gradual slowing before termination or temporary slowing of ventricular rate without termination indicates automatic tachycardia or atrial flutter/fibrillation (where vagal manoeuvres slow the rate of AV conduction temporarily, then the atrial activity continues when vagal tone withdraws). This distinction works both with vagal manoeuvres and with adenosine — abrupt termination = nodal re-entry; slowing or AV block revealing P waves = atrial origin; no effect = VT.

sections.body:
Sick sinus syndrome is the most common indication for permanent pacing. Understanding the different manifestations — sinus bradycardia, sinus pause, chronotropic incompetence, and the tachy-brady syndrome — determines who needs a pacemaker and which type.

## The sinus node — anatomy and blood supply

The SA node is a cigar-shaped structure (10–15 mm long) located in the right atrium at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrial appendage. Blood supply: sinus node artery (a branch of the RCA in ~60% of people, a branch of the LCx in ~40%). This explains why inferior MI (RCA territory) can cause acute sinus bradycardia.

## Sinus bradycardia

HR <60 bpm with normal P-QRS morphology and regular rhythm. Causes: (1) physiological — vagal predominance, athletes (resting HR 35–45 bpm is normal in a trained athlete); (2) pathological — hypothyroidism, hypothermia, raised ICP (Cushing response — bradycardia + hypertension), inferior MI (vagal surge), drugs (beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin, amiodarone).

When to treat: Only if symptomatic (syncope, presyncope, dizziness, fatigue limiting activity). Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia in a well patient requires no treatment — investigate the cause, remove offending drugs.

Acute treatment if symptomatic: IV atropine 500 µg (blocks parasympathetic → increases SA node rate). Repeat up to 3 mg. If atropine fails or cause is non-vagal: temporary transvenous pacing. Transcutaneous pacing (TCP) as bridge.

## Sinus pause and sinus arrest

Sinus pause: failure of the SA node to fire, resulting in a pause on the ECG without a P wave. A pause up to 2 seconds can be normal (especially during sleep or in athletes). Pauses >3 seconds are pathological.

Sinoatrial exit block: the SA node fires but the impulse fails to exit the node to the atrial myocardium. Type II SA exit block appears identical to sinus pause on surface ECG. Distinguished by EP study (intracardiac recording).

After the pause: if the pause is long enough, a subsidiary pacemaker (junctional or ventricular) escapes — the escape rhythm. The escape rate determines haemodynamic stability: junctional escape (40–60 bpm, narrow QRS) is better tolerated than ventricular escape (20–40 bpm, wide QRS, unreliable).

## Sick sinus syndrome (SSS) / Sinus node dysfunction

SSS is a clinical syndrome caused by intrinsic SA node disease (fibrosis, ischaemia, infiltration) producing: persistent inappropriate sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses >3 seconds, sinus arrest, chronotropic incompetence, and/or intermittent atrial tachyarrhythmias (the tachy-brady syndrome).

### Tachy-brady syndrome — the most dangerous SSS manifestation

AF (or another AT) terminates → the SA node, which has been suppressed by the rapid atrial rate (overdrive suppression), fails to recover promptly → a prolonged pause occurs → patient syncopises → eventually the SA node or a junctional escape pacemaker fires. This pause-termination pattern on a Holter monitor (fast AF → sudden termination → long pause → sinus restart) is pathognomonic of tachy-brady syndrome. Management challenge: AF requires rate/rhythm control (drugs slow the heart further) but the bradycardia also needs a pacemaker. The solution: implant a pacemaker first, then treat the AF aggressively.

### Chronotropic incompetence

Failure of the SA node to increase HR appropriately with exercise (failure to achieve ≥85% of maximum predicted HR = 220 – age). The heart cannot increase output with demand → severe exercise intolerance despite normal resting HR. Diagnosis by exercise stress test. Treatment: rate-responsive pacemaker (DDDR — the pacemaker detects body movement or respiratory rate and increases pacing rate accordingly).

## Pacemaker indications for sinus node dysfunction

| Indication | Class | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Symptomatic sinus bradycardia from intrinsic disease (not reversible cause) | Class I | Correlation between symptoms and bradycardia must be documented (Holter, loop recorder) |
| Symptomatic chronotropic incompetence | Class I | Use rate-responsive pacemaker (VVIR or DDDR) |
| Symptomatic sinus pauses >3 seconds awake | Class I | Asymptomatic pauses at night in athletes may be normal |
| Tachy-brady syndrome requiring antiarrhythmic drugs that worsen bradycardia | Class I | Pace first, then treat AF with drugs or ablation |
| Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia / pauses | Class III (not indicated) | No pacing benefit in the asymptomatic patient — symptom-rhythm correlation is the key requirement |

Key concept: Symptom-rhythm correlation is the essential requirement before permanent pacing for sinus node dysfunction — never pace for a rate or a pause alone
A Holter showing HR 35 bpm during sleep in an asymptomatic cyclist requires no treatment. The same HR causing syncope in an elderly patient requires a pacemaker. The ECG finding alone does not indicate pacing — the patient must be symptomatic AND the symptoms must coincide with the bradycardia. For intermittent symptoms, a 24-hour Holter may be insufficient — a 2-week external loop recorder or an implantable loop recorder (ILR, inserted subcutaneously, records for up to 3 years) may be needed to capture a symptomatic event and prove correlation.

Exam tip: Atropine works for vagally-mediated sinus bradycardia but NOT for intrinsic SA node disease. If the SA node itself is fibrotic (SSS), removing vagal tone (atropine) cannot make a dead node fire faster. In clinical practice: if atropine dramatically increases HR (e.g., HR 40 → 80 with atropine) → the bradycardia was vagally mediated (physiological or drug-induced) → less likely to need permanent pacing. If atropine has minimal or no effect on HR → intrinsic SA node disease → permanent pacemaker evaluation required. This "atropine test" is used informally at the bedside but formal EP study is the definitive assessment.

Checkpoint: A 72-year-old woman has three syncopal episodes — each occurring 10–20 seconds after the termination of rapid palpitations. Holter monitoring shows two episodes of PAF (paroxysmal AF) terminating with 4.5-second pauses before sinus rhythm resumes at 50 bpm. What syndrome is this, what is the immediate management priority, and why is starting flecainide alone insufficient?
Tachy-brady syndrome (a manifestation of sick sinus syndrome): paroxysmal AF → abrupt termination → SA node suppressed (overdrive suppression) → prolonged pause (4.5 seconds) → syncope → eventual sinus resumption. Immediate management priority: permanent pacemaker implantation first. The syncope is from the bradycardic pause, not the tachycardia. Once a DDDR pacemaker is implanted to provide a bradycardia safety net (it will pace at a minimum set rate, preventing the dangerous pause), she can then be safely treated for AF (catheter ablation, antiarrhythmic drugs, or rate control). Why flecainide alone is insufficient: (1) Flecainide (class Ic) will suppress AF but may itself cause SA node suppression (prolong sinus pauses) and the dangerous pause will be even longer. (2) Even if AF is suppressed, the underlying SA node disease remains — any future tachyarrhythmia termination will cause the same dangerous pause. (3) Flecainide is contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease (see Chapter 13) — her SA node disease may coexist with other structural pathology requiring exclusion. Sequence: pace first → assess AF management second.

sections.body:
AV block runs a spectrum from benign PR prolongation to complete electrical silence between the atria and ventricles. The critical distinction between Mobitz I and Mobitz II changes the management completely — one is generally benign, the other requires a pacemaker even without symptoms.

## First-degree AV block

PR interval >200 ms (5 small squares) with every P wave followed by a QRS. Not a "block" in the true sense — conduction is slowed, not blocked. Every P wave conducts. Location: usually the AV node.

Clinical significance: Usually benign. No treatment required. Causes: increased vagal tone, AV nodal drugs (beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin, amiodarone), inferior MI, Lyme disease (famous cause of high-degree AV block), infiltrative disease. A very long PR (>300 ms) may cause PR-related diastolic dysfunction (the atrium contracts so long before the ventricle that the tricuspid/mitral valve is already closing when atrial kick occurs → suboptimal haemodynamics). Some patients with symptomatic very prolonged PR may benefit from physiological pacing.

## Second-degree AV block — the critical distinction

### Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach)

Progressive lengthening of the PR interval with each beat until a P wave fails to conduct (dropped QRS), then the cycle resets. The key ECG features:

- PR lengthens progressively (but the increment gets smaller each beat — the biggest PR jump is from beat 1 to beat 2)
- RR intervals progressively shorten before the dropped beat (counterintuitive but follows from the smaller PR increments)
- The pause containing the dropped P wave is less than 2× the shortest RR interval
- Group beating pattern ("Wenckebach cycles" — groups of QRS complexes separated by pauses)

Location: AV node (suprahisian). The AV node fatigues with repeated stimulation (decremental conduction) — each successive impulse finds a more partially refractory AV node → longer delay → eventually block → recovery → cycle repeats.

Clinical significance: Generally benign. Common in young athletes (vagal predominance), inferior MI (reversible AV nodal ischaemia from RCA), drug effect. Usually does not progress to complete heart block. Responds to atropine (vagal origin).

### Mobitz Type II

Sudden, unexpected dropped QRS (non-conducted P wave) WITHOUT any preceding PR prolongation. The PR interval is constant in the conducted beats; then a P wave simply fails to conduct — without warning.

Location: infranodal — bundle of His, right or left bundle branch. The block is below the AV node. This is a different mechanism from Mobitz I — it reflects a diseased His-Purkinje system that fails to conduct intermittently, not the physiological fatigue of the AV node.

Clinical significance: Dangerous. Infranodal block can progress unpredictably to complete heart block — sometimes without warning. The escape pacemaker below the block is unreliable (ventricular — wide QRS, 20–40 bpm). Even asymptomatic Mobitz II requires permanent pacing because the risk of sudden complete heart block is high.

Key concept: Mobitz II always requires permanent pacing — even if asymptomatic. Mobitz I usually does not, unless symptomatic.
This is the most clinically important distinction in AV block management. Mobitz I: AV nodal, decremental, reversible, benign in most contexts. Mobitz II: infranodal, structural disease of the His-Purkinje system, unpredictable, can progress to complete heart block with a slow, unreliable ventricular escape rhythm. The escape rhythm determines survival after complete heart block: AV nodal block (junctional escape at 40–60 bpm, narrow QRS, reliable) is far safer than infranodal block (ventricular escape at 20–40 bpm, wide QRS, unreliable, often fatal without pacing). Never wait for symptoms before pacing Mobitz II — the first "symptom" may be cardiac arrest.

### 2:1 AV block — the diagnostic trap

Every second P wave fails to conduct — you cannot see PR progression (there is only one PR interval to observe). It may be Mobitz I or Mobitz II. Clues:

- Narrow QRS → likely AV nodal (Mobitz I) → observe; treat only if symptomatic
- Wide QRS (BBB morphology) → likely infranodal (Mobitz II) → treat as Mobitz II → pacemaker
- Responds to atropine (rate increases) → AV nodal → Mobitz I
- Worsens with atropine or with faster atrial rate → paradoxical worsening in infranodal block (faster rate hits the fatigued His-Purkinje system more often) → Mobitz II
- EP study (HV interval prolongation >70 ms) → confirms infranodal disease

## Third-degree (complete) AV block

No P waves conduct to the ventricles. Complete AV dissociation — the atria and ventricles beat independently. The atrial rate is fast (sinus at 60–100 bpm) and the ventricular rate is slow (determined by the escape pacemaker below the block).

ECG features: Atrial P waves at a regular rate. QRS complexes at a slower regular rate, completely unrelated to P waves (AV dissociation). P waves may appear to "march through" the QRS complexes.

Location of escape pacemaker determines QRS width and reliability:

- AV nodal block (congenital CHB, inferior MI) → junctional escape: narrow QRS, 40–60 bpm, relatively reliable
- Infranodal block (anterior MI, degenerative disease) → ventricular escape: wide QRS, 20–40 bpm, unreliable, fatal without pacing

Causes: Degenerative fibrosis of the conduction system (most common in elderly), acute inferior MI (vagal or ischaemic — usually reversible), acute anterior MI (septal necrosis — usually permanent, very high mortality), Lyme disease (temporary — high-grade block that typically resolves with antibiotics), cardiac surgery/valve procedures, infiltrative disease (sarcoid, amyloid, haemochromatosis), congenital (maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies → neonatal CHB).

## Pacemaker indications — AV block (ESC 2021)

| Indication | Class |
| --- | --- |
| Symptomatic complete (3°) or 2° AV block (Mobitz I or II) | Class I |
| Asymptomatic Mobitz II 2° AV block with narrow or wide QRS | Class I (pacemaker even without symptoms) |
| Asymptomatic complete AV block >10 s pause or ventricular escape <40 bpm | Class I |
| Asymptomatic Mobitz I (Wenckebach) 2° AV block | Class III (no pacing indicated) |
| 1° AV block alone (any PR interval) | Class III (no pacing indicated — unless very long PR with symptoms) |

## AV block in acute MI

- Inferior MI + AV block: RCA supplies the AV node. Block is AV nodal, usually Wenckebach, vagally mediated or ischaemic. Usually reversible within days. Temporary pacing if haemodynamically significant. Permanent pacing rarely needed (reserve for block persisting >7–14 days).
- Anterior MI + AV block: Septal branches of LAD supply the bundle branches. New LBBB or bifascicular block (RBBB + LAFB or LPFB) in anterior MI indicates septal necrosis. High risk of progression to complete heart block with a low, unreliable ventricular escape. Temporary transvenous pacing indicated. Most survivors require permanent pacing.

Exam tip: Bifascicular block + first-degree AV block does NOT reliably predict progression to complete heart block. A common exam misconception: "RBBB + LAFB + prolonged PR = trifascicular block → needs permanent pacemaker." This is wrong. Trifascicular block is a misnomer — the prolonged PR in this setting is usually from AV nodal disease, not true bilateral bundle branch disease below the AV node. True bifascicular disease with high risk of progression requires an EP study (HV interval >70–100 ms = infranodal disease → consider prophylactic pacing). The ECG finding alone does not mandate pacing in the absence of symptoms or documented infranodal disease.

Checkpoint: A 68-year-old man with syncope has this ECG finding: PR interval 220 ms in some beats; then an abrupt P wave that is not followed by a QRS (non-conducted P wave); other conducted beats have the same PR 220 ms as before. The QRS is 148 ms with LBBB morphology. What type of AV block is this, and what should you recommend?
Mobitz Type II 2° AV block. Key features confirming Mobitz II: (1) constant PR interval in conducted beats (220 ms) — no progressive prolongation; (2) sudden dropped QRS without warning; (3) wide QRS (148 ms) with LBBB morphology — confirming infranodal location of the block (the bundle of His or bundle branches). The LBBB indicates that the right bundle is the remaining functioning fascicle conducting those beats — the left bundle has failed. The block occurs when the right bundle also fails intermittently. Recommendation: permanent pacemaker — Class I indication even though he is symptomatic (syncope). If he were asymptomatic, the recommendation would still be permanent pacing (Class I for Mobitz II regardless of symptoms). Device choice: DDD pacemaker (dual-chamber — preserves AV synchrony). Given the existing LBBB and if EF is found to be ≤35% at echo, upgrade to CRT-D consideration. Urgent evaluation: do not discharge without either a temporary pacing wire (if haemodynamically unstable) or rapid inpatient permanent pacemaker implantation.
