sections.body:
Right-sided valve disease is dominated by secondary (functional) tricuspid regurgitation — the most common and most undertreated valve condition worldwide. Understanding when TR is a marker of pulmonary hypertension and when it is a primary driver of morbidity changes the management completely.

## Tricuspid regurgitation (TR)

### Primary vs secondary TR

Primary TR (leaflet-intrinsic pathology, ~10–20% of TR): infective endocarditis (right-sided, particularly in IV drug users), rheumatic disease (usually with concurrent MS/MR), carcinoid syndrome (5-HIAA → right heart fibrosis → "hockey stick" leaflets), myxomatous disease, Ebstein's anomaly (apical displacement of the tricuspid annulus → enlarged RA + small functional RV), radiation-induced, pacemaker/ICD lead-induced (lead impingement on leaflets).

Secondary (functional) TR (~80% of significant TR): annular dilation from RV dilation or AF → leaflets tethered apart → incomplete coaptation. Causes of RV dilation: left heart disease (LHF → pulmonary hypertension → RV pressure overload → RV dilation → TR), pulmonary hypertension (PAH, chronic thromboembolic PH), AF (atrial dilation → annular dilation → TR even without significant RV pathology).

### Grading and haemodynamic consequences

Severe TR produces: systemic venous congestion (elevated JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral oedema), reduced forward RV output → reduced LV preload → reduced CO → fatigue. The JVP in severe TR shows prominent CV waves (the regurgitant jet pressurises the RA/venous system during systole). Pulsatile liver (hepatic vein systolisation) is a bedside sign of severe TR.

Echocardiographic criteria for severe TR: vena contracta ≥7 mm, EROA ≥40 mm², regurgitant volume ≥45 mL, dilated IVC with reduced collapsibility (>21 mm, <50% collapse).

### Management of TR

- Secondary TR: treat the cause first. If left heart failure is driving pulmonary hypertension → GDMT and treat the left-sided lesion (MVR or AVR) — the TR may improve significantly post-surgery. If AF is the primary driver → AF ablation or cardioversion may reduce annular dilation.
- Surgical TR repair: ring annuloplasty at the time of mitral or aortic surgery. ESC Class I: moderate-severe TR in patients undergoing left-sided surgery; significant annular dilation (>40 mm) even with mild TR if undergoing left-sided surgery.
- Isolated surgical TR repair: historically avoided (high mortality) in advanced disease. ESC Class IIa: symptomatic severe primary TR refractory to medical therapy; severe TR with progressive RV dilation/dysfunction.
- Transcatheter tricuspid repair: rapidly evolving. TRILUMINATE Pivotal trial (TEER with TriClip) and CLASP TR trial — significant TR reduction, improved QoL. TRISCEND II trial (EVOQUE, transcatheter tricuspid replacement) — early strong results. These emerging technologies are opening the treatment of previously untreatable severe TR.

## Pulmonary stenosis (PS)

Pulmonary stenosis is almost always congenital (fused pulmonary valve leaflets) — calcific or rheumatic PS is rare. Severity correlates with the Doppler gradient across the RVOT/pulmonary valve:

- Mild PS: peak gradient <36 mmHg — typically asymptomatic, excellent prognosis without intervention
- Moderate: 36–64 mmHg
- Severe: ≥64 mmHg — intervention indicated

Treatment: percutaneous balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty (BPV) — the procedure of choice for congenital PS. Highly effective (gradient reduction from ~70 mmHg to <20 mmHg in most patients), low complication rate, avoids surgery in young patients. Surgery (pulmonary valvotomy/valvuloplasty) reserved for dysplastic valves (as in Noonan syndrome — not amenable to BPV) or significant sub/supravalvular PS.

Carcinoid syndrome and pulmonary stenosis: serotonin-mediated fibrosis → right heart involvement. Typically causes combined pulmonary stenosis AND regurgitation, often concurrent with tricuspid regurgitation and stenosis. The right heart valves are preferentially affected because serotonin is inactivated by the pulmonary vasculature before reaching the left heart. Management: surgery when severe symptoms — the carcinoid tumour prognosis often limits surgical candidacy.

## Pulmonary regurgitation (PR)

Physiological mild PR is present in virtually all adults and is haemodynamically insignificant. Pathological PR most commonly occurs after surgical or balloon repair of congenital pulmonary stenosis or tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) repair — the competence of the pulmonary valve is sacrificed during repair. Chronic significant PR → RV volume overload → RV dilation → RV failure (typically decades after TOF repair).

Pulmonary valve replacement (PVR) for post-TOF PR: indicated when RV end-diastolic volume index ≥160 mL/m² or declining RV EF (<47%). MRI is the gold standard for RV volume assessment. Transcatheter pulmonary valve implantation (TPVI — Melody valve, Sapien XT pulmonary) is now the preferred approach in suitable anatomy (previously placed bioprosthesis or conduit), avoiding re-operation in adults with repaired TOF.

Exam tip: Ebstein's anomaly — the tricuspid malformation with distinctive ECG and echo features. The tricuspid leaflets (especially the septal and posterior leaflets) are displaced apically into the RV → the RA is anatomically enlarged, incorporating part of the "atrialized" RV → true functional RV is very small. ECG: broad, notched P waves (large RA), RBBB, epsilon waves (in ARVC overlap), WPW is present in ~25% (right-sided accessory pathways common). Echo: apical displacement of the septal leaflet >8 mm/m² BSA from the MV annulus confirms the diagnosis. Severe Ebstein's → severe TR + cyanosis (from RA dilation → ASD/PFO → right-to-left shunting) → surgical repair (cone procedure). Ebstein's with WPW: the accessory pathway must be mapped and ablated before or at the time of surgery — WPW in Ebstein's is associated with AF and rapid conduction, risk of sudden death.

Checkpoint: A 65-year-old with severe TR (vena contracta 9 mm, massively dilated RA 7 cm, dilated RV with TAPSE 12 mm) and AF (HR well-controlled) is referred for consideration of isolated tricuspid surgery. His left heart is normal (echo: EF 62%, no significant MR or AS, PASP 38 mmHg — mildly elevated, not severely elevated). He is NYHA III on maximal diuretics. What are the two most important questions to answer before listing him for surgery?
1. Is the TR primary or secondary, and if secondary, can the cause be further modified? In this case: normal left heart with only mildly elevated PASP → the TR is unlikely to be driven by severe left heart disease or severe pulmonary hypertension. The mildly elevated PASP (38 mmHg) and AF could be causing secondary TR from AF-driven annular dilation — this is an increasingly recognised mechanism. If AF rhythm control has not been attempted (e.g., catheter ablation for AF) → this should be considered first, as AF ablation with restoration of sinus rhythm can reduce annular dilation and improve TR. If AF is permanent and refractory → proceed to surgical planning. 2. What is the RV function and is it still operable? TAPSE 12 mm indicates moderate-severe RV systolic dysfunction (normal ≥17 mm). The key question: is the RV dysfunction reversible (from the TR volume overload) or irreversible (intrinsic RV myocardial disease from chronic overload)? Severe irreversible RV dysfunction is a contraindication to isolated tricuspid surgery (the RV cannot survive the insult of surgery + bypass without further deterioration). Assessment: CMR for RV volume and EF; RV strain; RV end-diastolic volume. If RV EF <20% → extreme operative risk, may not survive. Consider transcatheter TR repair (TEER/TEER replacement — TRILUMINATE, TRISCEND) as an alternative to surgery in high-risk patients.
